title: Before increasing the AI coding budget, set the return you need
summary: Set output and quality thresholds before increasing an AI coding budget. Compare costs, peer benchmarks and the return needed to justify more spending.
body_markdown:
October’s engineering output per attributed AI dollar was 60.5% higher than September’s in the November 3, 2026[Weave Index snapshot](https://weaveos.com/data/return-on-token-spend) . Rescaled to $100 of spend, the average rose from **10.68 to 17.14 expert-effort output units** .


That is a substantial observed improvement. It is also a poor shortcut for deciding whether to raise a team’s budget. The population changes between months, so the figure cannot establish a 60.5% improvement within the same teams. Nor does an average reveal the return on the next dollar.


A useful budget request should name the work that more spending would make possible, and the result that would justify the increase.


## Compare AI cost per output with similar organizations


Weave combines cost per output with internal and peer comparisons. Its[AI report](https://docs.weaveos.com/reports/ai) shows cost per AI output by tool and cost per person, with billed and estimated amounts identifiable. The[Cost per output over time chart](https://docs.weaveos.com/annotations/benchmarks) can add peer reference lines and a percentile rank, so an engineering leader can compare the organization’s ratio with other Weave customers.


The default peer group uses organization size. An admin can select industry instead where enough organizations qualify; these are separate comparisons. The chart labels its population and falls back to size when an industry distribution is unavailable for the metric. Company and selected-team averages or medians provide internal reference points. Use these comparisons to investigate an unusually expensive workflow or a strong result worth understanding. They do not establish what an additional allowance will cause.


## Choose the decision before choosing the metric


**Raise an allowance.** First establish that the cap is constraining useful work. Record which tasks are delayed or abandoned when the allowance runs out. If the constraint is a review queue or unclear requirements, a larger allowance may leave it untouched.


**Change the model configuration.** Compare the same tasks under the candidate setups. Weave Router’s published benchmarks provide an example of the evidence a buyer should request:


Scroll horizontally if needed →


Benchmark Router GPT-6 Astra Cost per trial, Router / Astra


Terminal-Bench 4.0, 66 tasks 62.1% pass@2 60.6% pass@2 $5.22 / $10.03


SWE-Atlas Codebase QnA, 124 tasks 62.1% pass@2 66.1% pass@2 $2.31 / $5.04


Router solved one more Terminal-Bench task at roughly half the cost per trial. On SWE-Atlas, it cost less and solved five fewer tasks. Pass@2 allows up to two attempts per task; the listed costs are per trial. Router costs come from catalog-priced billing telemetry; Astra costs use vendor list pricing. The[methodology](https://weaveos.com/router/benchmark-methodology) records the settings, including Astra MAX versus Router high on Atlas. These results describe configuration tradeoffs, not a customer’s expected return from raising an allowance.


**Improve the workflow.** Find where spending fails to reach accepted work. Better task instructions, reusable skills or faster review may be the intervention to test. Measure the specific change against comparable work.


## Write down the break-even condition


If comparable spending rises 25%, quality-screened output must rise at least 25% to preserve output per dollar. If the share of output passing the same quality screen falls 10% relative to baseline, merged output must instead rise **38.9%** :


```text
Required merged-output increase = 1.25 / 0.90 - 1 = 38.9%


```


This is arithmetic under stated assumptions. It is a threshold for judging the result, not a forecast. Expert-effort output measures the work represented by code. It does not represent recorded working hours or cash savings.


A proposed study would test a 25% allowance increase within matched team pairs, using eight baseline weeks, eight treatment weeks and a 30-day quality follow-up. It would report changes in output and spending separately. That study has not run.


## Make the request specific enough to evaluate


[Telnyx’s operating model](https://weaveos.com/blog/telnyx-article) treats compute as capacity available to engineers. Weave’s[customer announcement](https://weaveos.com/blog/weave-raises-13.5m-series-a-to-build-engineering-and-token-intelligence) describes Telnyx using the platform to measure teams and agents and identify optimization opportunities. That is a useful operating example, separate from the proposed allowance experiment.


[Weave’s Token Intelligence](https://weaveos.com/products/token-intelligence) connects supported AI costs to engineering work, while Code Intelligence supplies inspectable output estimates. Together, they give a budget owner a way to examine both sides of an efficiency ratio.


For the next budget review, identify the tasks blocked by the allowance and set the output and quality thresholds the increase must meet. Compare the result with similar work completed under the existing allowance.
